title: Mixing things together
keyIdea: When you mix things, something changes. Flour and water stirred together turn into soft dough. Red and yellow paint stirred together make one new colour, orange, and blue and yellow make green. You cannot stir them back apart. Sugar stirred into water dissolves: you cannot see it, but it is still there, because the water tastes sweet. Sand stirred into water does not dissolve. It sinks to the bottom and you can still see it.

kid: Put flour in a bowl. Pour in water. Stir and stir. Now it is dough! It is soft and sticky.
Mix red paint and yellow paint. Stir. Now it is orange. Blue and yellow make green.
Stir sugar into water. The sugar goes away. But taste the water. It is sweet! The sugar is still there.
Stir sand into water. Then wait. The sand sinks to the bottom. You can still see it.
adult: In England this sits in the EYFS area Understanding the World. Development Matters (2021) asks 3 and 4 year olds to explore how things work and to talk about the differences between materials and the changes they notice. Mixing is also strong for Communication and Language: mix, stir, pour, change, sticky, dissolve and sink are the words to use. In the US, the Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework lists this under Scientific Reasoning: Exploration and Discovery.

What is really going on: flour soaks up water and the starch and proteins in it bind together, so a dry powder becomes a soft dough. Paints mix by colour: red and yellow make orange, blue and yellow make green, red and blue make purple. Sugar dissolves, which means it breaks up into pieces far too small to see and spreads all through the water. Sand grains do not dissolve, and they are heavier than the same amount of water, so they settle at the bottom.

Common mistakes to watch for: children often think two paints stay as separate spots; that dissolved sugar has gone for ever, or melted (melting needs heat; dissolving needs a liquid); and that sand will vanish like sugar if you stir hard enough. Tasting the sugar water and waiting for the sand to settle answer these better than telling.

In the lab your child pours water on flour and stirs it into dough, mixes red and yellow paint into orange, picks the two paints that make green, stirs sugar into water and tastes it, and stirs sand into water and waits for it to sink. Every step works with big buttons, or by tapping a pot and stirring round the bowl with a finger. Read the Challenge aloud together.

familyTip: Next time you bake, let your child pour and stir the flour and water and say what changed. Then stir a spoon of sugar into one cup of water and a spoon of sand or soil into another, wait a minute, and ask: which one can you still see?

visual.caption: Does it vanish in water, or can you still see it? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: Does not dissolve: you can see it

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stir flour and water into dough, mix paints into new colours, and see what sugar and sand do in water.

practice.prompt: You stir red paint and yellow paint together. What colour do you get?
practice.hint: Think of the colour of an orange you can eat.
practice.explain: Red and yellow mix into one new colour: orange.

practice.prompt: You put {n} spoons of flour in the bowl. How many spoons of flour?
practice.hint: Count 1 for each spoon of flour.
practice.explain: {n} spoons of flour went in the bowl. Count them one at a time.

practice.prompt: You stir {a} times. Then you stir {b} more times. How many stirs in all?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more stirs.

practice.prompt: You stir sugar into water. You cannot see it now. Is it still there?
choices: No, it has gone for ever
No, it went on the spoon
practice.hint: Taste the water. What does it taste like?
practice.explain: The sugar dissolved. You cannot see it, but the sweet taste shows it is still in the water.

pool.hint: One of them is the colour of the sky.
pool.explain: Blue and yellow make green. Red and yellow make orange, and red and blue make purple.

pool.prompt: You stir sand into water and wait. Where is the sand?
pool.hint: Does sand dissolve like sugar, or can you still see it?
pool.explain: Sand does not dissolve. It sinks to the bottom, and you can still see it.

pool.prompt: What do flour and water make when you stir them?
pool.hint: Think of what you use to make bread.
pool.explain: Flour and water stirred together make soft, sticky dough.

pool.prompt: You mixed red and yellow into orange. Can you get the red back out?
pool.hint: Did the spots of colour come back when you stopped?
pool.explain: Once paints are mixed they stay mixed. You cannot stir the red back out.

pool.prompt: {n} pots of paint are open. {k} more pots are shut. How many pots in all?
pool.hint: Count the open pots, then count on the shut ones.
pool.explain: {n} open pots and {k} shut pots make {=n+k} pots.

pool.hint: Which one makes the water taste sweet?
pool.explain: Sugar dissolves: you cannot see it, but it is still there. Sand and stones sink.

pool.prompt: You have {c} cups of water. You stir sugar into {s} cups. How many cups have no sugar?
pool.hint: Start at {c} and take away the {s} cups with sugar.
pool.explain: {c} take away {s} leaves {=c-s} cups with no sugar.

pool.prompt: What changed when you stirred the flour and water?
pool.hint: Was the flour dry or sticky at the end?
pool.explain: The dry flour soaked up the water and turned into soft, sticky dough.
